title: Gram-Schmidt Process (6.3)
description: Day 37: the Gram-Schmidt process in R^n, weighted inner products, and function spaces; normalizing; dependent vectors; and QR basics. 10 questions pulled per attempt from a pool of 60.

questions.prompt: In Gram-Schmidt, $u_2=v_2-\dfrac{\langle v_2,u_1\rangle}{\langle u_1,u_1\rangle}\,$ _____.
questions.explanation: You subtract the shadow of $v_2$ on $u_1$, which is that coefficient times $u_1$.

questions.prompt: Gram-Schmidt turns a linearly independent set into a(n) _____ set that spans the same subspace.
questions.explanation: The output vectors are pairwise orthogonal, and span$\{u_1,\dots,u_j\}=$ span$\{v_1,\dots,v_j\}$ at every stage.

questions.prompt: If a Gram-Schmidt step produces $u_k=0$, the original vectors were linearly _____.
questions.explanation: $u_k=0$ means $v_k$ is already in the span of the earlier vectors.

questions.prompt: To turn an orthogonal vector $u_i$ into a unit vector, divide it by its _____.
questions.explanation: $q_i=u_i/\|u_i\|$, where the norm is computed with the same inner product.

questions.prompt: In $A=QR$, the matrix $R$ is _____ triangular.
questions.explanation: Each $v_j$ is a combination of $q_1,\dots,q_j$ only, so $R$ has zeros below the diagonal.

questions.prompt: In $A=QR$ from Gram-Schmidt, the columns of $Q$ are _____.
$\dfrac{\langle v,u\rangle}{\langle u,u\rangle}\,u$ is called the _____ of $v$ onto $u$.
questions.explanation: It is the orthogonal projection of $v$ onto the line through $u$ (the 'shadow').

questions.prompt: In Gram-Schmidt, span$\{u_1,u_2\}$ and span$\{v_1,v_2\}$ are _____.
questions.explanation: Each $u$ is a combination of the $v$'s and vice versa, so the spans match at every stage.

questions.prompt: In $A=QR$ with independent columns, the diagonal entries of $R$ are the lengths $\|u_i\|$, so they are _____.
questions.explanation: $u_i\neq 0$ for independent columns, so each length is positive.

questions.prompt: Dot product. $v_1=(1,1)$, $v_2=(1,0)$. Find $\dfrac{\langle v_2,u_1\rangle}{\langle u_1,u_1\rangle}$ where $u_1=v_1$.
questions.explanation: $\langle v_2,u_1\rangle=1$ and $\langle u_1,u_1\rangle=2$, so the coefficient is $1/2$.

explanations: At every stage span$\{u_1,\dots,u_j\}=$ span$\{v_1,\dots,v_j\}$. Gram-Schmidt only changes the basis, not the subspace.

explanations: Project onto the new orthogonal vectors $u_1,u_2$, not the original $v$'s. The $v$'s are not orthogonal to each other, so their shadows overlap.

It is generally nonzero.
Since $v_1,v_2$ are not orthogonal, their shadows overlap and subtracting both over-removes or under-removes. Use $u_1,u_2$.

questions.prompt: Why is $u_2=v_2-\text{proj}_{u_1}v_2$ orthogonal to $u_1$?
choices: Taking the inner product with $u_1$ gives $\langle v_2,u_1\rangle-\frac{\langle v_2,u_1\rangle}{\langle u_1,u_1\rangle}\langle u_1,u_1\rangle=0$

questions.prompt: You may replace $u_2$ by $5u_2$ before computing $u_3$ and still get the same $u_3$.
explanations: The shadow $\frac{\langle v,u\rangle}{\langle u,u\rangle}u$ is unchanged if $u$ is scaled, so $u_3$ is exactly the same. Clearing fractions is allowed.

questions.prompt: Gram-Schmidt gives the same $u$'s no matter what order you list the $v$'s in.
explanations: The process depends on the order. Different orders produce different orthogonal bases (of the same span).

questions.prompt: A set of nonzero, pairwise orthogonal vectors is always linearly independent.
explanations: Dotting a dependence relation with $u_i$ kills every term but one, forcing each coefficient to be $0$.

questions.prompt: You run Gram-Schmidt on $v_1,v_2,v_3$ and get $u_3=0$. What does this tell you?
choices: $v_3$ is in span$\{v_1,v_2\}$, so the $v$'s were dependent
You made an arithmetic mistake, always
explanations: Unit length is unrelated.
If $v_3$ were orthogonal to the others, the shadows would be $0$ and $u_3=v_3\neq0$.
It can be a real signal, not an error: the remainder is $0$ exactly when $v_3$ lies in the span of the earlier vectors.

explanations: Orthogonality depends on the inner product. For $v_1=(1,1,1),v_2=(1,1,3),v_3=(0,3,1)$ the weighted output has $u_2=(-1,-1,1)$, while the dot product gives $u_2=(-2/3,-2/3,4/3)$.
